question.text: For imbalanced binary classification, does random oversampling of the minority class recover more minority-class recall than class weighting in logistic regression?

citation.title: Improving Loan Default Prediction Using Class Imbalance Techniques: A Comparative Study of SMOTE and Class Weighting Methods

data.claim: In the context of loan default prediction, a class-weighted logistic regression model achieved a recall of 0.66, which is substantially higher than the 0.17 recall achieved by SMOTE.
data.quote: The application of SMOTE improved recall to 0.17, while the class-weighted Logistic Regression model significantly increased recall to 0.66.

citation.title: LASSO-Regularized Binary Logistic Regression on Imbalanced Mode Choice Data

data.claim: In a mode choice dataset with class imbalance, applying SMOTE (oversampling) increased recall from 0.125 to 0.25, indicating an improvement in detecting the minority class.
data.quote: Results show that the LASSO model with SMOTE increased recall from 0.125 to 0.25

citation.title: The harm of class imbalance corrections for risk prediction models: illustration and simulation using logistic regression

data.claim: Random oversampling (as part of imbalance correction) does not improve model performance in terms of ROC curve area and leads to poorly calibrated models with overestimated probabilities for the minority class.
data.quote: The use of random undersampling, random oversampling, or SMOTE yielded poorly calibrated models: the probability to belong to the minority class was strongly overestimated. These methods did not result in higher areas under the ROC curve when compared with models developed without correction for class imbalance.

citation.title: Mass ratio variance majority cleansing and minority oversampling technique for class imbalanced

data.claim: A minority oversampling technique (specifically, mass ratio variance-based minority oversampling) improves recall compared to standard classifiers.
data.quote: The results of this proposed sampling technique improve recall over standard classifiers: a decision tree, a random forest, Linear SVM, and MLP on all synthesised datasets.

citation.title: Improving Minority Class Recall through a Novel Cluster-Based Oversampling Technique

data.claim: The proposed cluster-based oversampling technique significantly improves minority class recall, with a 30.54% increase in recall on the Delinquency Telecom dataset.
data.quote: An extensive evaluation across a diverse range of real-world data sets characterized by inter-cluster complexity demonstrates the superior performance of our method compared to that of existing oversampling techniques. Particularly noteworthy is its significant improvement within the Delinquency Telecom data set, where it achieves a remarkable increase of up to 30.54 percent in minority class recall compared to the original data set.

citation.title: GMO-AC: Gaussian-based minority oversampling with adaptive outlier filtering and class overlap weighting

data.claim: GMO-AC, a Gaussian-based oversampling method, improves performance metrics such as AUROC and G-mean, indicating better overall classification performance, including improved minority class detection.
data.quote: Experimental results show that GMO-AC yielded better AUROC and G-mean.

citation.title: Evaluating oversampling methods for imbalanced Arabic dialect identification

data.claim: SMOTE-RADIANT, a density-based oversampling method, significantly improves performance on minority classes (as measured by macro-F1) compared to the original data, and does not harm the majority class performance.
data.quote: In contrast, SMOTE-RADIANT yields a statistically significant macro-F1 improvement for LightGBM (0.8539 vs. 0.8526 on the original data) with a large effect size (r = 0.511), successfully rescuing minority dialects without degrading the majority class.

citation.title: A Comparative Study of Resampling Techniques for Handling Class Imbalance in Binary Classification

data.claim: Random oversampling (ROS) performs worse than other resampling methods in terms of PR-AUC, a metric closely related to recall in imbalanced classification.
data.quote: naïve ROS trails in every case.

data.description: The evidence directly comparing random oversampling of the minority class to class weighting in logistic regression is limited to a single study (E1), which reports that class-weighted logistic regression achieved a recall of 0.66, while SMOTE (a form of oversampling) achieved only 0.17. However, this study does not explicitly compare random oversampling to class weighting in the same model setup or on the same dataset, and the term 'random oversampling' is not clearly distinguished from SMOTE or other oversampling methods. Thus, the comparison between random oversampling and class weighting remains untested in a direct, controlled manner.

Most evidence on oversampling focuses on performance improvements in recall, but only a few studies (E2, E5, E6, E7, E8) report on recall improvements, and these are often in the context of different models (e.g., LASSO, decision trees, SVM, LightGBM) rather than logistic regression specifically. There is no evidence evaluating the performance of class weighting versus random oversampling in logistic regression across multiple datasets or in diverse real-world scenarios.

The evidence on the performance of random oversampling (e.g., random undersampling or random oversampling) is inconsistent—some studies (E3) claim it leads to poorly calibrated models and no improvement in ROC area, while others (E2, E8) show improvements in recall or PR-AUC. This contradiction suggests that the effect of random oversampling on recall is not reliably established, and the claim that it 'recovered more minority-class recall' than class weighting is not empirically supported across multiple contexts.

data.independent_variable: resampling method (random oversampling vs. class weighting)
data.rationale: The gap G1 identifies that no direct comparison exists between random oversampling and class weighting in logistic regression on the same dataset or under controlled conditions. Evidence E1 shows class weighting achieves 0.66 recall vs. 0.17 with SMOTE (a form of oversampling), but does not compare random oversampling to class weighting. Evidence E3 cautions that random oversampling leads to poorly calibrated models and no improvement in ROC, which may imply poor recall performance. This hypothesis directly addresses the gap by proposing a testable comparison under controlled conditions in logistic regression, using publicly available tabular data.
data.statement: In logistic regression models on imbalanced binary classification tasks, random oversampling of the minority class will result in a higher minority-class recall than class weighting, when evaluated on public tabular datasets with a minimum of 10% minority class prevalence.

data.independent_variable: resampling method (random oversampling vs. class weighting)
data.rationale: Gap G2 notes that most studies on oversampling focus on non-logistic models or general performance, and G3 highlights conflicting evidence: E3 claims random oversampling leads to poor calibration and no ROC improvement, while E8 states random oversampling performs worse than others in PR-AUC (a recall-related metric). This hypothesis tests whether the improvement in recall seen in other oversampling methods (e.g., SMOTE, cluster-based) is absent in random oversampling relative to class weighting in logistic regression, using macro-F1 as a recall-sensitive metric across diverse public datasets.
data.statement: On public tabular datasets with class imbalance, random oversampling will not improve minority-class recall compared to class weighting, as measured by macro-F1 score, when evaluated across multiple real-world datasets.

data.rationale: The hypothesis compares random oversampling to class weighting in logistic regression on imbalanced binary classification tasks with at least 10% minority class prevalence. The datasets breast_cancer_imb10 and digits_binary_imb10 meet the requirement of having a minority class prevalence of at least 10% (specifically, the minority class is subsampled to 10% of the majority). The control condition uses class weighting, which is directly referenced in the evidence (E1) as achieving 0.66 recall, while the treatment uses random oversampling (via the 'oversample' modifier), which is a form of random oversampling specified in the hypothesis. This design controls for model type (logistic regression), dataset imbalance, and evaluation metric (minority recall), allowing a direct comparison. A paired Wilcoxon test is used to assess the difference in minority recall between the two conditions, as it is appropriate for comparing two related samples (same model type, different hyperparameters). Five-fold cross-validation ensures robust evaluation, and multiple seeds ensure reproducibility and reduce variance due to randomness in data splits.

The hypothesis compares random oversampling against class weighting on macro-F1 score across public, imbalanced datasets. To isolate the effect of resampling methods while controlling for model and dataset bias, we use logistic regression as the base model. The control condition (class weighting) is the baseline, as per the hypothesis's expectation that class weighting is at least comparable or superior. The treatment condition (random oversampling) tests whether it improves macro-F1, which is sensitive to recall in imbalanced settings. We use 5-fold cross-validation to ensure robustness and apply paired Wilcoxon test to assess significant differences in macro-F1 scores between the two conditions. Seeds are specified to ensure reproducibility across runs. Datasets include both balanced and imbalanced versions to capture real-world variability. The inclusion of multiple datasets ensures generalization beyond a single case, addressing the gap in prior work (G2, G3) that notes limited real-world evaluation and conflicting results.

limitations: The comparison is limited to only two public tabular datasets (breast_cancer_imb10 and digits_binary_imb10), which may not represent broader real-world imbalances.

The design uses random oversampling, which is not directly equivalent to methods like SMOTE or cluster-based oversampling, and evidence (E3) indicates random oversampling leads to poorly calibrated models and no improvement in ROC.

The primary metric (minority recall) is not consistently improved by random oversampling, and evidence (E8) shows naïve ROS performs worse than other methods in terms of PR-AUC, a metric closely related to recall.
data.statement: The hypothesis is inconclusive because, across the two datasets, the mean difference in minority recall between random oversampling and class weighting does not consistently support a higher recall for oversampling. In breast_cancer_imb10, the mean difference is 0.0012 (95% CI: -0.025 to 0.0286, p_holm = 0.655), indicating no significant improvement, while in digits_binary_imb10, the mean difference is -0.0185 (95% CI: -0.0333 to -0.0074, p_holm = 0.0507), showing a decrease in recall with oversampling. Neither result meets the threshold for significance at alpha = 0.05 after Holm adjustment, and the direction of effect varies by dataset.
